title: Doing things for people — the -kan suffix
goal: Ask people to do things for you, and offer to do things for them, with *-kan*: *membelikan, membukakan, memasakkan*. Then meet the suffix's other big job, making things happen: *menyalakan, mematikan, memasukkan*.
bekal: ask and offer favours with *-kan*: *Tolong belikan saya…*, *Saya bukakan pintunya*
switch things on and off, put them in and turn them down: *menyalakan, mematikan, memasukkan, mengecilkan*
buy by the *ons*, the *ikat* and the *papan* at a traditional market

notes: **Boleh saya titip?** *Titip* is to leave something in someone's care, or to ask them to get you something while they're out. *Nitip, ya!* is how colleagues order snacks from whoever is going to the shop. Saying yes is ordinary neighbourliness; keeping track of the change is good manners.

**Mau dibelikan apa?** — literally "what do you want to be bought-for?" The *-kan* turns *beli* into a favour, and the *di-* makes Bu Endang the one who receives it. English needs a whole clause for this; Indonesian needs one word.

**Cabai rawit, bawang merah** — bird's-eye chillies, small and fierce, and shallots, literally "red onions". An ordinary onion is *bawang bombai*; garlic is *bawang putih*. ⚠️ *Cabai* is the standard spelling, but you will hear, and see on market signs, *cabe*.

**Tempe dua papan** — a *papan* is a board, and tempeh comes in flat slabs. Markets count things with their own words: *seikat bayam* (a bunch of spinach), *sebutir telur* (an egg). The first section below has more.

**Kasihan** is sympathy: "poor thing, what a shame". Say it to someone who is ill or unlucky: *Kasihan, Bu.* **Sekalian** means "while I'm at it, at the same time", and it is the key word for offering an extra favour.

**Matur nuwun** is Javanese for *terima kasih*, and in Yogya you hear it everywhere, from market sellers to *becak* drivers. Reply with *Sami-sami* (Javanese *sama-sama*) and you will earn a delighted laugh.

grammars.title: -kan for someone: the favour suffix
body: Add *-kan* to an action verb and the action is done **for** someone. The person who benefits comes straight after the verb, and the thing comes after the person.

head: Root
For someone
Example
English
rows: I'll carry your bag for you.

after: The order is fixed: verb, **person**, thing. *Membelikan Ibu obat* is "buy Ibu some medicine". If you want the thing first, use *untuk* or *buat*: *membeli obat untuk Ibu*. Both are correct and both are common.
⚠️ No favour, no *-kan*. *Saya membeli cabai* (I bought chillies) needs nothing more; *Saya membelikan cabai* on its own leaves every listener asking "for whom?"

grammars.title: -kan that makes things happen
body: The suffix's other job is to cause. It turns a state or a movement into something you do to an object, and this is how Indonesian switches things on and off, puts them in and turns them down.
after: ⚠️ Keep both *k*'s in writing when the root ends in *k*: *memasukkan*, *menaikkan*. *Memasukan* with a single *k* is one of the commonest spelling mistakes in Indonesia, on shop signs and in newspapers alike.
💬 In speech the *me-* drops as usual: *Saya masukkan ke kulkas*, *Nyalakan lampunya*. In Jakarta *-kan* itself often becomes *-in*: *masukin, nyalain, matiin* (Unit 19).

dialogs.intro: Wednesday, ten to ten, in the meeting room. A delegation from a partner university in Jakarta is due at ten, and Mbak Nur is running the room like air-traffic control.

notes: **Tolong nyalakan proyektornya** — a request with a *-kan* verb, bare like every request. *Nyalakan* comes from *nyala* (burning, alight): lamps, stoves, engines and computers are all *dinyalakan*. *Hidupkan* ("make alive") is a common alternative, especially for engines.
**Sudah saya nyalakan** — Unit 4's object-first pattern with a *-kan* verb. Nothing changes: the object (here understood), *sudah*, the doer, then the bare verb with its suffix.

**Coba saya cek** — "let me have a look". *Coba* (try) softens an offer or a request: *Coba lihat* (have a look), *Coba saya tanya dulu* (let me ask first). It is one of the most useful little words in the language.

**Ahli teknologi** — *ahli* is an expert. Bayu is joking, of course: plugging in a cable hardly makes Sarah an engineer. Indonesians often tease with over-the-top compliments, and the right reply is a laugh, not a correction.

**Kirim or kirimkan?** Both mean "send", and in daily use they are nearly interchangeable. *Kirimkan* leans a little more on the thing travelling towards someone; Unit 6 sets *-kan* against *-i* (*mengirimi Rina surat*) and makes the difference clear.

**Jangan dimatikan** — a negative request in the passive, softer than *Jangan matikan*. **Kecilkan** (make smaller) is how you turn down the air conditioning, the volume or the flame; *besarkan* (make bigger) turns them up.

grammars.title: Requests with -kan, blunt and polite
body: Office Indonesian has three levels for the same request. The bare *-kan* verb is an instruction; *tolong* makes it a request; the passive makes it gentler still.
after: When you name the object in a gentle passive request, it usually sits between *tolong* and the verb: *Tolong proyektornya dinyalakan*, *Tolong pintunya dibukakan*.
Between colleagues, *tolong* + verb is the default. The bare instruction is for real hurry or for children, and even that turns friendly with a *ya* on the end: *Matikan, ya.*

sections.title: At the market: amounts and counters

blocks.text: Traditional markets sell by weight, by bunch and by piece, and each has its own little word. The prefix *se-* means "one": *sekilo, seikat, sebutir*.
⚠️ An *ons* in Indonesia is 100 grams, not an English ounce of 28. *Tiga ons daging* is 300 grams of meat, which is a very different dinner.

blocks.title: Titip: the favour system
items: *Nitip, ya!* ("get me one too!") is how snacks, coffee and lunch reach people stuck at their desks.
Whoever goes out brings back the change; the others pay up at once. Leaving a *titipan* unpaid overnight is bad form.
*Titip salam* (send my regards) uses the same verb: *Titip salam buat Rina, ya!*
Before a trip, asking *Mau titip apa?* (want me to bring you anything?) is thoughtful and very Indonesian.

blocks.text: Every gadget in an Indonesian house is switched on, off, up and down with a *-kan* verb. The spoken forms drop *me-*, as usual, and usually add *-nya*.

*Ngecas* comes from English "charge", and everybody says it: *HP-ku lagi dicas* (my phone's charging). The standard *mengisi daya*, literally "filling up power", is what the box the charger came in says.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
